crimlab

Statistical methods for courts, corrections, policing, forensics and sociolegal research. The computations run in a compiled C++17 core with a plain C interface (src/crimlab.h); the R functions check their arguments and call it. Where an identity or a bound has a machine-checked proof in Lean, proof() names the theorem.

crimlab in one minute: a veil-of-darkness table, a reported odds ratio checked against every labelling of its table, a clearance paradox, a categorical audit, a posterior from a likelihood ratio, hot spots, spatial autocorrelation, the command-line program, and the theorems behind a function

It is written for researchers and analysts in criminology, sociolegal studies, policing, corrections and forensic science who need these quantities computed correctly and want to know what each one does and does not show. vignette("crimlab") walks through one example from each family.

What it takes

The functions work on summary data, not on raw records:

  • counts by group: stops, searches, uses of force, offences recorded and cleared, residents, offenders and victims;
  • individual outcomes coded 0 or 1, with a group or a decision for each person: release, sentence, reconviction;
  • allele frequencies and genotypes at one or more loci;
  • likelihood ratios from validation comparisons whose source is known;
  • networks as edge lists of labels (who offended with whom, who passed what to whom), or incident tables that list the offenders of each incident.
  • point locations of incidents, planar or longitude and latitude (vectors, tables or sf points), with times, weights or counts by area;
  • risk scores with outcomes and groups, trace-evidence measurements, event time windows, reported figures, matched-pair differences and counts over time.

What it asks

  • Disparities: does visibility change who is stopped, what an odds ratio says about risk, whether hit rates can show bias, how a disparity per resident splits into contact and force.
  • Forensics: how rare a DNA profile is, what a likelihood ratio is worth and what it is not, how well a system’s ratios are calibrated, kinship, paternity, mixtures and database searches.
  • Policing: why an aggregate clearance rate can fall while every offence type clears better, what a proxy for exposure allows, what misrecorded group membership does, regression to the mean at hot spots.
  • Corrections: what incapacitation prevents, what a release rule’s failure rate can be when only the released are seen, mean time in custody from current stays, and what observational data alone say about a sentence’s effect.
  • Networks: who co-offends with whom, who sits between groups, which offenders form the core and the communities of a network, and how cleanly it splits in two.
  • Places: where incidents centre and how far they spread, whether they cluster more than chance, where the hot spots are, whether places close together have similar rates (Geary’s C, the Getis-Ord G, local Moran), whether incidents close in space are close in time, and where to search first for the base of a series.
  • Methods from the forensic and sociolegal literature: the fairness of a risk tool by group, the weight of glass and other trace evidence, when an event known only within a window happened, whether reported figures follow Benford’s law, how strong hidden bias must be to explain a matched result away, and group-based trajectories of offending.
  • Counts and rates: rate ratios between groups from Poisson and negative binomial regression with an exposure, adjustment and cluster-robust or GEE standard errors (cntreg()); rates and proportions by group with their ratios and differences, exact and approximate intervals and over-representation (grprr()); directly standardised rates (dastd()); observed over expected counts with funnel limits and empirical Bayes shrinkage (sirex()).
  • Tables: cross-tabulation of records or of an aggregate table’s counts, with chi-square and likelihood-ratio tests, Fisher’s exact test, Cramer’s V with its interval, and the share on the diagonal (ctabx()).
  • Time and contagion: Hawkes processes fitted to event times with a choice of kernels and baselines, their residuals and simulation (hwkfit(), hwkres(), hwksim()).
  • Marked, mutual and space-time contagion: ETAS (etasf()), multivariate Hawkes processes (mvhwk()) and the space-time Hawkes process of crime (sthwk()).
  • Series: the trend in a count series as a rate ratio, by Mann-Kendall and Theil-Sen, by period and season (trndrr()); step changes and Pettitt’s test (stpcp()); CUSUM surveillance (cusrv()); the correlation of two series at lags (xcser()).
  • Durations: Kaplan-Meier curves, medians and the log-rank test, of durations or of the gaps between repeat events (kmrec()).
  • Patrol operations: Larson’s hypercube queue (hypq()) and the square-root law of response distance (sqrtlw()).
  • Hot spots: the Short-D’Orsogna-Brantingham model of repeat burglary, simulated as agents or as its continuum limit (sdbsim()), and the threshold at which hot spots form (sdbthr()).
  • Presets: how the columns of a published dataset (Ontario segregation and deaths-in-custody tables, use-of-force files, Special Investigations Unit cases, Structured Intervention Unit tables, Toronto incident layers) feed these functions, so that cntreg(clprep(data, "otis-c01-cnt")) gives the published analysis (clprep()). The risk-tool audits (fairdf(), tmpaud(), calaud(), scrdsp()) take presets the same way. Presets describe layouts and ship no data.
  • Audits of risk tools and predictive policing: how a tool’s decisions differ between groups, with intervals (fairdf()), over time and place (tmpaud()); whether an algorithm ranks areas in the order of what was then recorded there, and whether the disagreement follows the areas’ groups (calaud(), scrdsp()); whether similar people get similar scores (lipaud()); what a noisily recorded base rate says about the true one (nsbnd()); the false positive rate the other rates force (impfpr()); which pairs a noisy ranking orders (rnkres()); the Oaxaca-Blinder split of a gap (oaxbd()); and simulated records with a known disparity to try them on (fairsim(), nordet()). They describe what a tool or an agency did, not why.
  • Checks: which labelling of a table reproduces a reported odds ratio, risk ratio or risk difference (relchk()), and what the functions here would make of categorical inputs before an analysis (catchk()).
  • Police-reported crime: a severity-weighted index of counts by offence, per population and against a base period (crsev()), and a composite of standardised counts that ranks areas on several kinds of crime at once (zcomp()).
  • Concentration: how unequally incidents or placements fall across places and people, how much of a Gini coefficient comes from units with none, what chance alone would show and how distinct places grow (cconc()), and the tail index of a heavy-tailed count (hilltl()).
  • The dark figure: how many offenders or incidents no list records, from two or three overlapping lists (crcap()), and what a victimisation survey and recorded crime together say about the crime that is never recorded (dkfig()).
  • Published tables: what a banded category, a rounded or suppressed cell, or a change between two published years can and cannot say (bandx(), pbbnd(), yoypx()).
  • Courts: what a judge-leniency design identifies and how far it rests on monotonicity (jdgiv()), whether judges’ leniency rankings hold across pairs and groups of cases (jmono()), and how sentences sit against a mandatory minimum (mmshr()).
  • Life course and the pipeline: what an aggregate age-crime curve can and cannot say about types of offenders (agemix()), the cumulative risk of a first arrest or admission by age (cumrsk()), and rates between stages of the justice system with a lag (jpipe()).
  • Segregation: how many placements, and how many people, meet the Mandela Rules’ definitions of solitary confinement and prolonged solitary confinement, by year or region and under each denominator (mndla()).
  • Custody and courts as stocks and flows: how the population held, admissions and the length of stay determine each other (stkflw()), how long stays are (lostay()), what a backlog implies about the time cases take (bklog(), dktflw()), how long cases take from grouped times (lftab()), and how people move between states (trnmat()).

Algorithms

Every method is a published one, cited on its help page; none is new, and the package does not claim to be the first implementation of any of them in R. What it adds is a single checked implementation: arguments are checked in R and again in the compiled kernels, quantities that overflow or cancel in the obvious formula are computed in a stable form, and most functions rest on identities or bounds proved in Lean, which proof() names.

Speed

dev/bench.R times each function against every other package found that computes the same quantity, on fixed seeded inputs and at sizes met in practice, after checking that the two give the same values; dev/bench-net.R does the same for the network functions. The search for those packages, with the reason each candidate does or does not compute the same quantity, is inst/bench/counterparts.csv (written by dev/cpart.R). rmorie, the maintainer’s own package, is timed too but reported apart: it is not another package. Where no package computes a quantity, the function is timed against rmorie or a base-R implementation of the formula, and no claim is made against the field. The tables, with the machine, its load during each run and the spread over three runs, are inst/bench/bench.md (and bench.csv) and inst/bench/net.csv. The lists below are written by the same scripts from those tables. The spatial functions and the learners have speed tables of their own, inst/bench/sp.csv (dev/bench-sp.R) and inst/bench/dml.csv; the three name their columns alike.

Faster, by at least a tenth, than every other package found that computes the same quantity, at every size timed: gtmp(), mixlr(), cllr(), cllrmin(), eceplt(), clrsmp().

Not faster than another package at some size timed: kinidx(), patidx(), lrcal().

No other package found that computes the same quantity, so no claim of speed against the field: vodtst(), orrisk(), outtst(), dspbm(), dyadrt(), expbnd(), misrd(), rtmhs(), incap(), incapr(), sellab(), losbnd(), sntbnd(), hzdsel(), lrpost(), dbsrch(), tipplt(), proof(). Of these, compared with rmorie, the maintainer’s own package: faster at every size timed: vodtst(), orrisk(), outtst(), dspbm(), dyadrt(), expbnd(), misrd(), rtmhs(), incapr(), sellab(), losbnd(), sntbnd(), hzdsel(); not faster at some size: incap(). Compared with a base-R implementation of the formula: faster at every size timed: dbsrch(), proof(); not faster at some size: lrpost(), tipplt().

Networks, against igraph, sna, tnet and netmem: faster, by at least a tenth, than every package that computes the same measure, at every size timed, counting only the measure on a graph the other package has already built: ntcls(), ntevc(), ntcmp(), ntlvn(), ntmod(), ntbrk(), coofg(). Not faster at some size by that count: ntdeg(), ntbtw(), ntcore(); of these, counting the building of the other package’s graph from the same labels, which crimlab’s time includes, faster at every size: ntcore(). No other package found: ntchg().

Life cycle

Experimental. This is a development version: function names, arguments and results may change before a first release.

Installation

From GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("rootcoder007/crimlab")

The package needs a C++17 compiler and no R package beyond those that ship with R.

Examples

Disparities in policing 

library(crimlab)

# veil of darkness: does visibility change who is stopped?
vodtst(day = c(white = 600, black = 400), night = c(white = 700, black = 300))

# the same counts from a data frame: groups are matched by name, never by
# position, and a table with day and night columns can be given whole
stops <- data.frame(race = c("white", "black", "white", "black"),
                    light = c("day", "day", "night", "night"),
                    n = c(600, 400, 700, 300))
vodtst(xtabs(n ~ race + light, stops), ref = "white")

# the risks, and the relative risk, behind an odds ratio
orrisk(or = 3, rate = 0.4, share = 0.5)

# outcome test: stop and hit rates at a search threshold
outtst(q = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), t = 0.3)

# force per resident = contact per resident x force per contact
dspbm(pop = c(a = 9000, b = 1000), contact = c(a = 900, b = 300),
      force = c(a = 9, b = 6))

# offending rates per offender and per offender-victim pair
pop <- c(a = 800, b = 200)
dyadrt(count = outer(pop, pop) / 1000, pop = pop)

Clearance rates 

# both offence types clear better in B, yet B's aggregate rate is lower
clrsmp(clra = c(minor = 90, serious = 20), reca = c(minor = 100, serious = 50),
       clrb = c(minor = 19, serious = 60), recb = c(minor = 20, serious = 140))

Corrections 

# custody against a community sentence, with no assumption about who got which
y <- c(1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0)
z <- c("community", "community", "custody", "custody", "custody",
       "community", "custody", "community")
sntbnd(y, z, treat = "custody")

# a release rule scored from the outcomes of those the judge released
sellab(y = c(0, 1, 0, NA, NA), rel = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE),
       rule = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE))

DNA match statistics 

# match probability with the Balding-Nichols correction
gtmp(p = c(D3 = 0.1, vWA = 0.2), q = c(0.3, NA), hom = c(FALSE, TRUE),
     theta = 0.03)

# a likelihood ratio needs a prior before it is a probability
lrpost(lr = 1e6, prior = 1 / 5e6)

# a match found by searching a database
dbsrch(mp = 1e-9, n = 5e6, pop = 3e7)

Kinship, paternity and mixtures 

kinidx(g1 = c(12, 14), g2 = c(12, 14), freq = c(0.1, 0.2), rel = "sibling")
patidx(child = c(12, 14), father = c(14, 15), freq = c(0.1, 0.2),
       mother = c(12, 12))

p <- c(a = 0.1, b = 0.2, c = 0.05, d = 0.15)
mixlr(p, np = character(0), xp = 0, nd = c("c", "d"), xd = 1)

Performance of likelihood ratios 

same <- c(50, 200, 8, 0.5)
diff <- c(0.01, 0.2, 1.5, 0.001)
cllr(same, diff)
cllrmin(same, diff)
lrcal(same, diff)
tipplt(same, diff)
eceplt(same, diff)

Co-offending networks 

# offenders recorded together in an incident are tied, weighted by the
# number of incidents they share
inc <- c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5)
off <- c("ana", "ben", "cy", "ana", "ben", "cy", "dee", "dee", "eli", "fay")
g <- coofg(inc, off)
e <- g$edges
ntdeg(e$from, e$to, w = e$w, nodes = g$nodes)
ntbtw(e$from, e$to, nodes = g$nodes)
ntlvn(e$from, e$to, w = e$w, nodes = g$nodes)
ntbrk(e$from, e$to, grp = c(ana = "x", ben = "x", cy = "x", dee = "y",
                            eli = "y", fay = "z"), nodes = g$nodes)

Spatial input 

# planar coordinates (metres, say): two vectors, a matrix or a data frame
# with columns x and y; longitude and latitude only with lonlat = TRUE
set.seed(1)
p <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100, 500, 50), y = rnorm(100, 800, 30))
cgstat(p)
sdell(p, c = 2)

ll <- data.frame(lon = c(-79.40, -79.38, -79.35), lat = c(43.64, 43.66, 43.65))
webpt(ll, lonlat = TRUE)          # the centre comes back in degrees
hvdist(ll, c(-79.38, 43.65))      # great-circle metres
eqproj(ll)                        # equal-area metres for the planar functions

# sf points go in directly; their CRS must agree with lonlat
s <- sf::st_as_sf(ll, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
cgstat(s, lonlat = TRUE)
# and plain results go back to sf
sf::st_as_sf(eqproj(ll), coords = c("x", "y"))

The planar functions assume Cartesian coordinates in one length unit and return lengths in that unit; functions with a lonlat argument project longitude and latitude to metres themselves (an equal-area projection about the points’ centre) and return centres in degrees; functions that take a study rectangle (win) take planar coordinates only. All are two-dimensional.

Hot spots, space-time and journey to crime 

set.seed(2)
x <- c(rnorm(40, 0, 0.3), rnorm(40, 6, 0.3), runif(40, -5, 10))
y <- c(rnorm(40, 0, 0.3), rnorm(40, 6, 0.3), runif(40, -5, 10))
fzmode(x, y, r = 0.5)                               # points within 0.5 of each
nnhclu(x, y, area = 225, p = 0.05, minpts = 5)$clusters
kmpart(x, y, k = 3, seed = 1)$cen
stacel(x, y, win = c(-5, 10, -5, 10), r = 0.75, top = 10, minpts = 5)$clusters
mantst(x, y, t = seq_along(x), nsim = 199, seed = 1)
mantst(x, y, t = seq_along(x), nsim = 199, seed = 1, metric = "manhattan")
hdbang(x, y, v = fzmode(x, y, r = 0.5))      # head-bang smoothing
crwalk(cbind(x = x[1:10], y = y[1:10]), h = 2, seed = 1)$msd
# clusters relative to a population at risk; zones as counts at centroids
rnnhcl(x, y, base = cbind(x = runif(500, -5, 10), y = runif(500, -5, 10)),
       h = 1, minpts = 5)$clusters
fzmode(x[1:20], y[1:20], r = 1, count = rpois(20, 3))

# a search priority over a grid, not evidence about any person
s <- jtsurf(c(2, 3, 4), c(2, 4, 3), win = c(0, 6, 0, 6), nx = 30, ny = 30,
            type = "negexp", par = c(1, 1), mode = "lik")
jtacc(s$prob, win = c(0, 6, 0, 6), base = c(3.2, 2.9))

Spatial weights and autocorrelation 

set.seed(4)
p <- cbind(x = runif(60), y = runif(60))
v <- ifelse(p[, 1] > 0.7 & p[, 2] > 0.7, 5, 1) + rnorm(60, sd = 0.3)
w <- spwt(p, k = 5)                    # or type = "band", or "contig"
gearc(v, w)                            # Geary's C
gorg(v, spwt(p, type = "band", d = 0.2, style = "raw"))   # global G
head(lmorn(v, w, nsim = 199, seed = 1))                    # local Moran
locgi(v, spwt(p, type = "band", d = 0.2, style = "raw"))  # local G*
dirmn(p, origin = c(0.5, 0.5))         # directional mean from an origin

Near repeats, hot spots, scans and spatial regression 

set.seed(5)
p <- cbind(x = runif(300, 0, 3000), y = runif(300, 0, 3000))
t <- runif(300, 0, 365)
knxnr(p, t = t, ds = c(100, 200), dt = c(7, 14), nsim = 99, seed = 1)
k <- kdsurf(p, nx = 40)                # intensity surface, MASS::kde2d() x n
k$regions                              # smallest areas holding 50%, 90%
dbscn(p, eps = 150, minpts = 4)$sizes
hsper(p, prd = rep(2021:2023, 100), cell = 500, top = 0.1)$periods
ebshr(c(40, 12, 9, 25, 7, 31, 5, 18))$est     # the expected fall of hot spots
kscan(p, t = t, r = c(150, 300), tw = c(14, 30), nsim = 49, seed = 1)$cl
w <- spwt(p, k = 5)
gmoran(p[, 1] + rnorm(300, sd = 500), w, nsim = 99, seed = 1)
bvmor(p[, 1], p[, 2], w, nsim = 99, seed = 1)
f <- sarml(p[, 1] / 1000 + rnorm(300), p[, 2] / 1000, w, durbin = TRUE)
spill(f)                               # direct, indirect and total effects
crossk(p, marks = rep(c("a", "b"), 150), i = "a", j = "b",
       win = c(0, 3000, 0, 3000), r = c(100, 200))$k
qdrtst(p, win = c(0, 3000, 0, 3000), nx = 3)
dissix(cbind(a = c(90, 80, 10, 5), b = c(10, 20, 85, 95)))$d
bufas(p, site = cbind(1000, 1000), comp = cbind(2500, 2500), r = 300)$n

Risk tools, trace evidence, time and data screens 

set.seed(3)
g <- rep(c("a", "b"), each = 100)
y <- rbinom(200, 1, ifelse(g == "a", 0.3, 0.5))
s <- plogis(rnorm(200, ifelse(y == 1, 0.8, -0.8)))
fair(s, y, g)$met                     # error rates and predictive values by group

rswp(rnorm(50, 0.5), gam = c(1, 1.5, 2))   # how much hidden bias explains it away
bnft(bdig(exp(runif(500, 0, 10)))$dig)$stat
gstr(matrix(rpois(100, 2), 10))[1:3, ]
sptst(rpois(30, 10), rpois(30, 10), nboot = 199, seed = 1)$glob
### Audits of risk tools and predictive policing

```r
d <- fairsim(4000, nareas = 24, bias = 0.5, seed = 1)  # a known disparity
fairdf(d$det, d$group, base = "A")$tab[, c("group", "dp", "di", "dilo", "dihi")]
calaud(d$area, d$risk, d$det, d$group, nperm = 499, seed = 1)$groups
scrdsp(d$risk, d$group)$anova
nsbnd(c(a = 0.35, b = 0.55), a = 0.1, b = 0.2)$pairs   # ordered under noise?
impfpr(p = c(a = 0.3, b = 0.5), ppv = 0.6, fnr = 0.25)  # Chouldechova
oaxbd(d$risk, d$truth, d$group, ref = "A")$dec

Checking reports and inputs 

# which reference group and event give a reported odds ratio of 0.44?
tab <- matrix(c(20, 10, 80, 90), 2,
              dimnames = list(c("A", "B"), c("yes", "no")))
relchk(tab, 0.44, ref = "B", event = "yes")

# missing values, unused and rare levels, labels that differ by case, and
# the reference level a default would take
d <- data.frame(sex = c("Male", "male", "Female", "Female", NA),
                custody = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE))
catchk(d, nmin = 2)

Proofs 

proof("vodtst")

Checking the proofs

The Lean 4 files are in inst/lean (installed under system.file("lean", package = "crimlab")). With elan installed:

cd inst/lean
lake exe cache get   # prebuilt Mathlib, about 5 GB
lake build

A build with no error and no sorry is the check.

Licence

Apache License 2.0 with LLVM Exceptions; see LICENSE. The SPDX identifier is Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception. The exception lets compiled code that embeds the kernels be redistributed without the attribution conditions, and settles linking with GPL-2 software.

Python

py/ holds a Python package, also named crimlab, that compiles the same kernels from src/ and gives the same functions, argument names and results; its tests check every number against the R package. It has no runtime dependencies. Install it from a clone with pip install ./py; see py/README.md for how inputs are matched by name and the few differences from R.
